Consult Summary:
- Acute asthma exacerbation suspected in a patient with known atopy, presenting with wheeze and shortness of breath over 2–3 days, partially responsive to albuterol; plan includes stepping up controller therapy, inhaler guidance, and near-term GP review with red-flag instructions.

History:
- Presenting complaint
  - Tightness in chest with shortness of breath starting ~2–3 days ago during a run; currently short of breath with brisk walking, wheezing, and coughing.
  - Uses a blue (short-acting beta-agonist) inhaler with limited relief; reports using it daily during symptoms and to prevent symptoms (morning/evening).
  - No sputum production; no fever reported.
- Symptom pattern and timeline
  - Onset during running; symptoms persist at rest and with activity; not clearly improving with current SABA use.
  - Peak flow not repeatedly measured during episode; patient reports a normal baseline peak flow around 380 (L/min).
- Exacerbating/relieving factors
  - Exacerbated by exertion (running); relief limited with SABA; ongoing daily use suggests poor control during this period.
- Associated symptoms
  - Wheeze, cough; no significant sputum; no chest pain described.
- Past asthma history
  - Asthma diagnosed; last attack 3–4 years ago; previous GP management emphasized ongoing inhaler use.
  - Not admitted to hospital for asthma; no prior oral steroids or antibiotics for asthma.
  - Prior asthma review with nurse ~2 years ago; generally well controlled until this recent period.
- Atopy and allergies
  - History of eczema and hay fever; family history of asthma (brother); sister with eczema.
  - Allergies: hay fever (environmental/environmental allergen) noted; drug allergies none reported.
- Medications
  - Salbutamol (blue inhaler) inhaler used as needed; frequency described as during symptoms and sometimes every day for prevention.
  - Beclomethasone (brown inhaler, Clenil) inhaler used daily; plan to increase to four puffs twice daily.
  - Topicals: Cetraben (emollient) and Hydrocortisone; Bactroban mentioned in conversation.
  - Dose/frequency specifics for current SABA use not consistently documented; plan includes explicit frequency guidance.
- Social History
  - Not specified beyond family history and atopy.
- Family History
  - Brother with asthma; sister with eczema.
- Review of systems
  - No systemic signs of infection reported; no chest X-ray or lab results discussed.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma (history with intermittent control; last major attack several years ago)
- Eczema
- Hay fever/allergic rhinitis (atopy)
- Family history of asthma and eczema

Medications:
- Salbutamol inhaler (blue) — dose/route/frequency not documented; used as needed; in this episode used more frequently (every 2–4 hours during symptoms).
- Beclomethasone inhaler (Clenil, brown) — currently used daily; plan to increase to four puffs twice daily; dose/route/frequency for current use not precisely documented.
- Cetraben (emollient) — usage not quantified.
- Hydrocortisone (topical) — usage not quantified.
- Bactroban (topical antibiotic) — usage not quantified.
- Allergies: hay fever (environmental); no drug allergies reported.

Social History:
- Not documented beyond family history and atopy.

Family History:
- Brother with asthma.
- Sister with eczema.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Exam findings: Not recorded.
- Chest/respiratory exam planned but not yet performed in transcript.
- Peak flow: Baseline reported by patient as ~380 L/min (current measurement not performed during visit).

Investigations:
- Peak expiratory flow (baseline): ~380 L/min (patient-reported as normal for them).
- Chest examination and formal spirometry/peak flow during the visit were planned but results not provided in transcript.
- No labs or imaging mentioned.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Acute asthma exacerbation (likely mild-to-moderate) in a patient with known asthma and atopy, currently with insufficient control despite SABA use.
- Consistent with DDx considerations including atopy-driven asthma and possible viral or exercise-related triggers; manage with escalation of controller therapy and symptomatic relief with SABA; red-flag instructions provided for deterioration.

DDx Integration (brief):
- Acute asthma exacerbation
  - Supporting: Known asthma; wheeze and SOB; ongoing SABA use with symptoms; plan to increase ICS and adjust SABA.
  - Opposing: No prior hospitalization; last attack several years ago.
- Viral/URTI-triggered bronchospasm with asthma flare
  - Supporting: Onset over 2–3 days with cough and dyspnea; atopy present.
  - Opposing: No fever or purulent sputum reported.
- Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (with underlying asthma)
  - Supporting: Symptoms started during running; exertional dyspnea/wheeze.
  - Opposing: Symptoms persist at rest beyond exercise period; not limited to post-exercise.
- Allergic/atopic airway inflammation
  - Supporting: Strong atopic history (hay fever, eczema) and family history; ongoing daily ICS/reliever use.
  - Opposing: None specific to current episode; needs clinical correlation.

Issue 1: Acute asthma exacerbation
- Diagnosis/Impression: Acute asthma flare in the setting of existing asthma with recent symptom onset and suboptimal relief from SABA.
- Plan:
  - Inhaled corticosteroid (brown inhaler, Clenil/beclomethasone): increase to four puffs twice daily.
  - Short-acting beta-agonist (blue inhaler, salbutamol): advised use during symptoms; advised to limit use to a maximum every 2–4 hours; if frequent use persists, consider escalation.
  - Safety netting: seek urgent care (A&E) if breathing worsens or cannot maintain comfort; current plan to see a GP in next few days.
  - Follow-up: arrange GP appointment within a few days; in interim, consider a tele- or in-person check; ensure chest exam and peak flow are documented at follow-up.
  - Investigations: perform chest examination and peak flow measurement during follow-up or sooner if available; results will guide need for antibiotics or systemic steroids if indicated.
  - Patient education: review inhaler technique, reinforce adherence to controller therapy, and discuss red flags prompting ED presentation.

Issue 2: Asthma management optimization and follow-up
- Plan:
  - Schedule a formal asthma review with a GP in the next few days.
  - Emphasize adherence to daily inhaled corticosteroid therapy; confirm dose and regimen at follow-up.
  - Reassess peak flow and symptoms to determine control level and need for or adjustment of controller therapy.
  - Consider escalation to longer-term controller strategies if symptoms persist.

Issue 3: Atopy-related conditions (allergic rhinitis/hay fever and eczema)
- Plan:
  - Continue current atopy-related therapies (emollients; topical hydrocortisone as indicated; Bactroban if indicated).
  - Monitor for any triggers that may exacerbate asthma (allergic rhinitis management may help overall control).

General plan and safety-netting:
- Increase brown inhaler dose: four puffs twice daily.
- Increase SABA use during symptoms: up to every 2 hours as needed; if symptoms require frequent use, seek urgent care.
- Seek urgent medical care (A&E) if breathing worsens or cannot manage symptoms at home.
- Book an in-person GP review within a few days; obtain a formal asthma assessment, including chest exam and peak flow measurement.
- Provide patient education on recognizing warning signs and when to escalate care.

Quality checks (documented at bottom):
- Missing but clinically expected elements: Vitals and formal physical examination not documented in the transcript; no objective imaging or labs obtained.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified; DDx items align with transcript.
- Transcript quality: Conversation largely coherent but with some ambiguity regarding exact inhaler dosing history; cross-checked with plan (increase ICS, SABA guidance) to ensure consistency.

Notes:
- All information reflects content from the transcript and the provided DDx with no additional unverified data.
- American English, concise, professional tone maintained throughout.
